title: Detection of Domains
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary takeover of existing domains and subdomains rather than registration of new ones, because an established domain already carries reputation and user trust. A hijacked registration account, an expired domain or a dangling subdomain record can each hand an attacker control of a name that your users and customers believe in. The telemetry that makes it visible is certificate transparency monitoring, registrar and name server audit records, passive resolution history and inventory checks for host names that point at unclaimed cloud services. It fails because the takeover usually happens at a third party, so the first external sign is often a customer complaint or a certificate you never requested.

beginner.definition: A domain is the name that people type to reach your service, such as your company name. A subdomain is a smaller name that sits under it. An attacker who takes over a name can receive your mail or copy your website. This detection looks for signs that a name you own is no longer fully under your control.
beginner.whyItMatters: Users check the name, not the certificate owner. An established domain has years of trust behind it, so a message or a link from it is rarely questioned. Attackers therefore prefer to take over a name instead of buying a similar one. The most common route is a forgotten subdomain that still points at a cloud service nobody claims. Another is an expired registration caused by a payment failure. Both are cheap for the attacker and expensive for you. Recovery takes time, and the trust loss lasts much longer.
howItWorks: A monitoring service watches certificate transparency logs for every name under your domains.
It also reports resolution history, so you can see when a record starts pointing somewhere new.
The detection compares each discovered name with your inventory of owned names and services.
Cloud service responses are checked to find host names that point at unclaimed resources.
Registrar records are reviewed for expiry dates, contact changes and transfer requests.
An unknown name, an unclaimed target or an unexpected transfer request raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a block of flats with a shared letterbox panel. Each flat has a slot, and the postman trusts the panel. If one flat is empty, a stranger can label that slot with his own name. The owner never collects the keys. Mail for the building still arrives at the panel, so nothing looks broken. The stranger now reads letters meant for that flat. A forgotten subdomain is that empty slot, and your detection is the manager who checks the labels every week.
takeaways: A trusted name is worth more to an attacker than a new one.
Forgotten subdomains and expired registrations are the usual way in.
Certificate transparency is the fastest independent view of your names.

objectives: Explain why attackers prefer to take over an existing domain.
Identify the records that reveal a subdomain takeover.
Describe how certificate transparency monitoring exposes new names.
Build a process that keeps the name inventory complete.
Prioritise remediation for dangling records and expiring domains.
dataSources: Certificate transparency monitoring results for all names inside your registered domains
Registrar audit records for transfer requests, contact changes and expiration warnings
Passive domain name system resolution history showing where each subdomain points over time
Cloud service error responses or banner text collected for host names in your inventory
Public address and host name inventory matched against records that still point at retired services
logic: The pattern is a name that belongs to your organisation resolving to a resource that no longer exists, or a registration change on a domain you own that no internal team requested. The fields that must be correlated are the fully qualified name, the record type and target, the certificate issuer and validity dates, the registrar account used and the internal owner recorded for that name. Benign cases include staging names that are intentionally pointed at a test service and provider migrations that reuse an address. The malicious case is a record whose target returns a service specific error meaning the resource is unclaimed, or a certificate issued for a name that appears in no inventory.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Subdomain Record Points at Unclaimed Cloud Resource
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: 'http_probe_result'
#     hostname|endswith: '.corp.example'
#     cname_target_claimed: 'false'
#   filter_owned:
#     hostname|in: 'approved_hostname_inventory'
#   condition: selection and not filter_owned
# level: high
falsePositives: A cloud storage bucket that is intentionally empty and returns an authorisation error instead of a page.
Staging subdomains that are deliberately pointed at a test environment without a certificate.
A provider migration where an old record still exists during a short planned overlap period.
Internal only names that appear in public name server data by mistake after a zone transfer.
tuningNotes: Keep the host name inventory linked to the team that owns each service, and review it after every decommission. Filter names that are recorded as intentionally parked and the short overlap windows agreed with providers. Scope the alerting rule to names that carry mail or authentication records. If you narrow the rule to production names only, you lose the staging subdomain that an attacker can still use to phish staff, so keep a weekly report that covers every name in the zone.
